title: Does what the newborn senses explain why birth beside the parent protects populations?
question: Over eight studies, populations whose newborns are placed beside a stranger went extinct in 88/96 runs and those placed beside the parent in 30/96. Q6-Q9 changed which attacks and shares land within the family in four ways and never clearly removed the protection (16/48 extinct with the intervention vs 15/48 without). The remaining candidate is sensory: beside the parent, a newborn's 'other agent' sensors respond to its parent rather than to a stranger. This study makes the parent invisible to its offspring's sensors, and in a second condition also makes offspring invisible to their parent.
background: Interventions change sensing only; attacks, shares and placement are unchanged. blind_to_parent=True: an agent's three 'other agent' sensors never respond to its own parent. blind_to_family=True: also, a parent's sensors never respond to its own offspring. Newborns are placed beside the parent in both. stranger is a reference only. Interpretation rule, fixed in advance: what the newborn senses explains the protection if H50a or H50b is supported; sensing between parent and offspring in either direction matters if H50c or H50d is supported; if none is, neither sensing nor the family attacks tested in Q6-Q9 explain it. No pilot was run. Seeds 2700-2711 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: With offspring blind to their parent, populations beside the parent die out sooner
With offspring blind to their parent, populations go extinct more often
With parent and offspring blind to each other, populations die out sooner
With parent and offspring blind to each other, populations go extinct more often
